title: Primary education programme to be split into six projects as ADB eyes non-formal education
excerpt: The state minister for primary education told ADB the government has decided in principle to break PEDP-5 into six separate projects.

image.alt: A tin-roofed government primary school building in rural Bangladesh
image.credit: Nurunnaby Chowdhury (Hasive) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
The government has decided in principle to divide the Fifth Primary Education Development Programme (PEDP-5) into six separate projects, State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj told the Asian Development Bank (ADB) on 12 November, The Business Standard reported.

Hajjaj met ADB Country Director Qingfeng Zhang at the Secretariat. He said the split would make implementation and financing more specific and easier to track against results. Zhang said ADB wants to expand its support for non-formal education and skills development, alongside its current work on primary education quality.

Key points

  • PEDP-5 was approved by ECNEC on 10 November at Tk 41,090 crore. The six projects and how the budget will be shared between them have not been announced.
  • Hajjaj said the ministry is now focusing on classroom teaching and learning outcomes, after years of spending on buildings, teacher training, curriculum and school grants.
  • He asked development partners for more long-term money for non-formal education, skills training and lifelong learning.

Why it matters

Earlier primary education programmes ran as a single sector-wide programme, with donors pooling money behind one results framework. Six separate projects could mean separate procurement, separate project offices and separate donor arrangements. For education NGOs and consultants, that changes where opportunities sit, and it may make it easier for donors such as ADB to fund a specific piece, such as non-formal education, without joining the whole programme.

What to watch

The names, budgets and lead agencies of the six projects, and whether the World Bank's $300 million for primary education is tied to one of them.
